plot_extraction.response_text:
Sam Small, urged by his sister to advise her twenty-one-year-old son Joe against marrying too young, enlists his friends Ginger Dick and Peter Russet. Joe cheerfully agrees with their cynical claims about women and marriage but insists his own fiancée, Miss Gill, is uniquely perfect.

When the three men meet the attractive Miss Gill, Ginger decides to prove Joe foolish by winning her affection. He takes her to the zoo, where she flirts with him, hints at romantic interest, and tearfully reveals that she urgently needs three pounds. Ginger lends her the money, but when he kisses her, she slaps him and has him thrown out.

Unaware of the trick, Peter bets he can also take Miss Gill out. He succeeds, returns three pounds poorer, and likewise conceals that she slapped him. Soon afterward, Joe proudly displays a silver watch, chain, and gold ring that Miss Gill has bought him. Ginger and Peter compare experiences and realize that she extracted three pounds from each of them, rejected both after encouraging them, and used their money to purchase Joe’s gifts.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the manner of a comic oral anecdote, framed by a night-watchman whose sight of a young couple prompts him to recall a cautionary tale about courtship. This frame establishes a conversational, performative voice: the narrator appears to be speaking directly to an implied listener, digressing freely and treating the story as practical evidence for his rueful maxim that people regret both marrying and not marrying. The embedded narrative remains largely in this storyteller’s idiom, so that even third-person description feels like speech rather than formal literary narration.

Its most conspicuous stylistic feature is eye-dialect representing working-class London and seafaring speech. Aspirates are regularly dropped—“’e,” “’er,” “’ad”—while forms such as “wot,” “ses,” “arter,” “agin,” “fust,” “gal,” “afore,” and “p’r’aps” reproduce pronunciation and colloquial grammar. Double negatives, non-standard agreement, compressed phrases, and nautical vocabulary reinforce the speakers’ social milieu. The dialect is dense but systematic, giving the prose a strong audible quality and making distinctions between narration and dialogue deliberately slight: the storyteller speaks much as his characters do. Repeated dialogue tags such as “ses Ginger” and “ses Peter” imitate the rhythms of spoken recitation.

The syntax is generally plain, additive, and paratactic. Sentences often join actions with “and” or “but,” moving from one small incident to the next in a loose chain: characters arrive, argue, make wagers, take outings, and return to compare results. Descriptions are concise and concrete rather than lyrical. Longer sentences accumulate comic details, while short exchanges accelerate arguments and expose contradictions. Repetition is central to the rhythm. Ginger and Peter echo one another’s opinions, each repeats the same courtship pattern, and phrases or situations recur with small variations until the concealed design becomes apparent.

The narrative perspective is outward-looking and behaviorally focused. Characters are revealed through speech, gestures, spending, boasting, and reactions rather than psychological analysis. The narrator occasionally supplies motives, but these are usually simple and comic, and the reader is often encouraged to understand more than the men do. Expressions such as “pore Ginger,” “old Sam,” and “careless-like” introduce amused evaluative commentary without interrupting the tale. Stock physical images—Ginger returning “like a dog with its tail between its legs,” or opening and shutting his mouth “like a dying fish”—turn humiliation into visual comedy.

Dialogue carries most of the characterization. Sam, Ginger, and Peter present themselves as worldly authorities on women, yet their vanity and credulity continually betray them. Their claims to romantic experience are transparently self-flattering, and their advice is undermined almost as soon as it is given. Joe’s youthful certainty initially appears foolish, but the older men prove no less susceptible. Miss Gill speaks in a softer, more calculated register, using hesitation, modest refusal, emotional disclosure, and apparent vulnerability to direct Ginger and Peter without openly asking for money. Her repeated reluctance to accept assistance is part of the manipulation, though the narration withholds explicit confirmation until the final revelation.

The humour depends chiefly on dramatic irony, masculine self-deception, reversal, and delayed disclosure. The men believe they are rescuing Joe from a scheming woman, then imagine they are successfully seducing her, while the reader gradually suspects that they are being managed. Their misogynistic generalizations are comically redirected against them: the supposed experts on female deceit cannot recognize an elementary confidence trick because vanity persuades each that he is uniquely attractive. Physical comedy—the roundabout, boat-swing, rifle gallery, wrong bus, elephant ride, and slap—supplements the verbal irony. Understatement intensifies the effect, as embarrassing or costly events are recounted in the same matter-of-fact tone as ordinary errands.

The structure is tightly cumulative despite its casual oral surface. It opens with a general observation about romantic folly, introduces three self-appointed cynics, tests their wisdom against Joe’s engagement, and then sends Ginger and Peter through nearly identical episodes. Each outing follows a miniature arc of flirtation, emotional confession, financial sacrifice, and rejection. The apparent repetition sets up the final punch line: Miss Gill has used the six pounds obtained from the two men to buy Joe a silver watch and chain and a gold ring. Peter’s closing admission that she slapped him too completes the parallel and ends the story abruptly at the moment of maximum comic recognition.

The setting is rendered through familiar social locations rather than atmospheric description: sailors’ lodgings, Poplar streets, public houses, sweet shops, omnibuses, fairground attractions, the Zoological Gardens, and the Crystal Palace. Money, leisure, and courtship are closely linked. Small sums, wagers, treats, fares, jewellery, and the men’s recently earned pay provide both material stakes and comic motivation. The world is socially specific, bustling, and modestly urban, with the sailors’ shore leave contrasting with their habitual life at sea.

Overall, the tone is genial, sardonic, and unsentimental. The story mocks youthful idealism, middle-aged vanity, romantic cliché, and boastful masculine solidarity without becoming severe. Its governing method is to let characters condemn folly in others and then enact the same folly themselves. The resulting style combines vernacular storytelling, economical characterization, patterned repetition, and a carefully concealed comic payoff.

generation.response_text:
I see a young chap and a gal leaning over the railings there, and I don’t disturb ’em. If they was to topple into the river through leaning too far, I might tap ’em on the shoulder; but so long as they keep their feet and don’t obstruct the pavement, it ain’t no business o’ mine. Young people must learn, same as old ones did afore ’em.

Some men regret getting married, and some regret not getting married, and the sensible ones regret both. I knew a ship’s carpenter once who kept out of it till he was sixty-five, and then married a widow with four grown-up sons. He spent the first part of his life wishing ’e had a family, and the last part wishing somebody else ’ad ’em. There’s no pleasing everybody.

Talking o’ marriage reminds me of Sam Small and the time ’is sister’s boy, Joe, got engaged to Miss Gill. Sam’s sister lived at Poplar, and Joe was her only son. He was twenty-one, with a clean collar every Sunday and more confidence than a man of forty, and when he told ’is mother that he was going to marry, she spoke to Sam about it.

“You’re ’is uncle,” she ses. “You ought to advise ’im.”

“I’ve never been married,” ses Sam.

“That’s why,” she ses. “A man that’s been married might be prejudiced.”

Sam scratched ’is chin and looked thoughtful. He was staying ashore with Ginger Dick and Peter Russet at the time, the three of ’em having been paid off from the brig *Martha Ann* with more money in their pockets than was good for ’em.

“I’ll talk to ’im,” he ses. “I’ll put ’im right.”

“You won’t make ’im angry?” ses his sister.

“Me?” ses Sam. “I shall just reason with ’im quiet and manly.”

He went off that evening to the lodging-house where Ginger and Peter was sitting with their boots on the mantelpiece, smoking and wondering what to spend their money on next. Ginger had already bought a concertina he couldn’t play, and Peter had got a new overcoat with a velvet collar that made ’im look like an undertaker on ’oliday.

“I want your ’elp,” ses Sam.

Peter took his boots down at once.

“Not if it means lending,” he ses.

“It ain’t,” ses Sam. “It’s my sister’s boy, Joe. He’s going to get married.”

Ginger shook his head and clicked ’is tongue.

“At twenty-one,” ses Sam.

Ginger clicked it agin, louder.

“Pore young feller,” ses Peter. “Can’t nothing be done?”

“That’s wot I want you two for,” ses Sam. “You know women.”

Ginger sat up and pushed his cap back. If there was one thing Ginger liked, it was being told ’e knew women. He had been walking out with three at different times, and two of ’em had married other men while he was at sea. The third had moved and forgot to leave ’er address.

“I know ’em root and branch,” he ses.

“So do I,” ses Peter. “I can tell wot a woman’s thinking by the way she looks at another woman’s bonnet.”

“You come round to my sister’s with me to-morrow night,” ses Sam. “We’ll talk to Joe. Three experienced men ought to be able to save one boy.”

“Easy,” ses Ginger.

They went round next evening, and Joe, who was sitting in the parlour with a photograph in front of ’im, welcomed ’em very hearty. He was a good-tempered young chap, and instead of getting annoyed when Sam mentioned the engagement, he smiled all over ’is face.

“So you’re thinking of getting married?” ses Sam, severe-like.

“I’m not thinking,” ses Joe. “It’s settled.”

“There’s time to unsettle it,” ses Peter.

Joe shook his head.

“Twenty-one,” ses Ginger. “Why, at twenty-one a man don’t know whether ’e wants tea or coffee till ’e’s swallowed it.”

“I know wot I want,” ses Joe.

“Course you think you do,” ses Sam. “That’s where the danger is. Wot do you know about gals?”

Joe thought a moment.

“Not much,” he ses, “except Miss Gill.”

Ginger gave a groan.

“They’re artful,” he ses. “You bear that in mind. Artful ain’t the word for it, but it’ll ’ave to do till somebody makes a stronger one.”

“And extravagant,” ses Peter. “A gal’ll look at a sixpenny ribbon for ten minutes, and then spend half a crown because she’s tired of standing.”

“And changeable,” ses Sam. “They change their minds oftener than a ship changes ’er course in a fog.”

Joe listened very respectful.

“I dare say you’re right,” he ses.

The three of ’em looked at each other, rather taken aback.

“Dare say?” ses Ginger. “We know.”

“I’m sure you do,” ses Joe. “You’ve had experience.”

Peter coughed and pulled down his waistcoat.

“More than enough,” he ses.

“I knew a gal once,” ses Ginger, “as said she’d wait for me for ever. I was away eleven months, and when I come back she’d been married six and was talking about naming the baby after ’er husband.”

“Shocking,” ses Joe.

“And I knew one,” ses Peter, “as told me she didn’t care for money. She proved it by spending mine.”

“Terrible,” ses Joe.

Sam leaned forward and tapped ’im on the knee.

“That’s why we’re warning you,” he ses. “You take three men of the world like us. We ain’t got nothing to gain by it. We don’t want to see you throw yourself away.”

“I’m much obliged,” ses Joe. “And everything you say is true—about most women.”

“Most?” ses Ginger.

“All except Miss Gill,” ses Joe, smiling agin. “She’s different.”

Ginger’s face fell.

“They always are,” he ses.

“I mean it,” ses Joe. “She’s sensible, steady, affectionate, economical, and as innocent as a child.”

Peter looked at Sam, and Sam looked at Ginger.

“How old?” ses Peter.

“Twenty,” ses Joe.

“Twenty!” ses Ginger. “And innocent! Why, a gal of twenty knows things a man of fifty wouldn’t like to ’ear.”

“Miss Gill don’t,” ses Joe. “She’s never had another sweetheart.”

“How d’you know?” ses Sam.

“She told me.”

Ginger got up and walked twice round the table. Then he stopped in front of Joe.

“P’r’aps she told the others the same,” he ses.

“There wasn’t no others,” ses Joe. “You’ll understand when you meet ’er.”

“We don’t want to meet ’er,” ses Sam.

“I do,” ses Ginger, quick.

Sam turned and stared at ’im.

“Only to judge,” ses Ginger. “For Joe’s sake.”

Peter said he wouldn’t mind judging too, and Joe, who seemed pleased at their interest, arranged for ’em to meet Miss Gill on the following Saturday evening.

She came to tea at Sam’s sister’s, and when she entered the room all three men stopped talking. She was a small, neat-looking gal, with bright eyes and a quiet way of smiling as if she knew something pleasant and was considering whether to tell it. She shook hands with Sam and Peter, but when Ginger held out ’is hand she gave the least little start and looked at ’im twice.

Ginger noticed it. So did Peter. Sam was looking at the cake.

Miss Gill sat beside Joe and listened while the three men told stories about foreign parts. Ginger spoke most. He had never been farther east than Rotterdam, but before tea was over he had given Miss Gill a very good idea of Bombay, Yokohama, and the habits of South Sea Islanders. Peter tried to correct ’im once or twice, but Ginger talked louder.

“You must have had a very adventurous life, Mr. Dick,” ses Miss Gill.

“I ’ave,” ses Ginger, looking at ’er. “But lonely.”

“Lonely?” she ses, soft-like.

“Terrible,” ses Ginger.

Joe passed ’im the bread and butter and told ’im to keep ’is strength up.

When Miss Gill went home, Joe walked with ’er. The moment the door shut behind ’em, Ginger turned on Sam.

“You’re right,” he ses. “This marriage must be stopped.”

“Why?” ses Peter.

“Because that gal ain’t suited to Joe,” ses Ginger. “A nice gal, mind you, but not suited.”

“She seemed very fond of ’im,” ses Sam.

“That’s only ’er innocence,” ses Ginger. “She don’t know ’er own mind yet.”

“And you do, I s’pose?” ses Peter.

“I know human nature,” ses Ginger. “Did you see the way she looked at me?”

“She was wondering whether Bombay was in Japan,” ses Peter.

Ginger took no notice.

“I could take that gal away from Joe in a week,” he ses. “Not that I want to. I wouldn’t hurt the boy’s feelings for anything. But it might be a kindness to show ’im ’ow mistaken he is.”

Sam rubbed his nose.

“I don’t like it,” he ses.

“It’s for ’is good,” ses Ginger. “If she can be took away by me, she ain’t fit to marry ’im.”

“And if she can’t?” ses Peter.

Ginger smiled.

“She can,” he ses.

By Monday evening he had arranged to meet Miss Gill the following Wednesday. He did it very artful, telling Joe that he wanted to talk to ’er about a little surprise for ’im. Joe thanked ’im, and Miss Gill, after looking doubtful for some time, consented to go with Ginger to the Zoological Gardens.

Ginger bought a new necktie for the occasion and had ’is boots cleaned twice. On Wednesday morning he went out before breakfast, and Peter, who was watching from the bedroom window, said he walked past the house three times afore he remembered which way the omnibus went.

He met Miss Gill at two o’clock. She was dressed very quiet, but Ginger said afterward that everybody in the Gardens looked at ’er. The truth was they looked mostly at Ginger, because ’e had put his new necktie on with the wide end behind.

They started with the lions, and Miss Gill shivered and moved closer to ’im when one of ’em roared.

“Don’t be frightened,” ses Ginger. “He can’t get out.”

“I know,” she ses. “But I’m so nervous.”

“If he did get out,” ses Ginger, swelling up, “I’d know wot to do.”

“Would you?” she ses, looking at ’im.

“I’d stand between you and ’im,” ses Ginger.

Miss Gill looked grateful, and Ginger, backing away careless-like to show how little he thought of lions, trod on a child’s hoop and sat down. The child screamed, its mother screamed louder, and Ginger gave ’em twopence to go away.

After that they saw the monkeys, and Miss Gill said one of ’em reminded ’er of somebody. Ginger asked who, and she laughed and said she wouldn’t tell ’im for worlds. He laughed too, though he didn’t see much in it, and bought ’er a bag of nuts.

At the elephant-house she said she had always wanted to ride on an elephant, and Ginger paid for both of ’em. He didn’t want to ride ’imself, but he wasn’t going to let ’er go alone. The elephant got up at both ends separately, and Ginger clutched the seat with one hand and Miss Gill with the other.

“Ooh!” ses Miss Gill.

“It’s all right,” ses Ginger, with ’is eyes shut.

“You’re not afraid?” she ses.

“Me?” ses Ginger. “I was just thinking.”

The elephant took six steps and stopped. Ginger opened one eye.

“It’s very high,” ses Miss Gill.

“Nothing when you’re used to it,” ses Ginger.

Then the elephant moved agin, and Ginger’s hat dropped off. A boy picked it up and wore it round the enclosure till Ginger offered threepence. By the time they got down, Ginger said elephants was stupid beasts and ought not to be encouraged.

Miss Gill was full of apologies for suggesting it.

“I’ve been such a trouble to you,” she ses.

“Trouble?” ses Ginger. “I’d ride an elephant to the North Pole for you.”

She turned ’er head away, but not afore he saw ’er smile.

They had tea and buns, and then Ginger took ’er on a roundabout outside the Gardens. Miss Gill chose a horse, and Ginger, not to be outdone, chose one alongside. The machine started, and every time he tried to speak to ’er his horse went up while hers went down. He called “Miss Gill!” fourteen times, and once caught hold of an elderly lady’s bonnet by mistake. When it stopped he got off the wrong side and walked round twice looking for Miss Gill, who was standing behind ’im.

After that they tried a boat-swing. Ginger didn’t like it from the first, but Miss Gill said it was so romantic, and he sat opposite ’er and pulled the rope. In less than a minute he wished ’e hadn’t. Miss Gill laughed, with ’er hair blowing about ’er face, while Ginger grew pale and swallowed hard.

“Higher!” she ses.

Ginger pulled once more and then shut ’is eyes.

When the swing stopped he remained seated.

“Aren’t you coming?” ses Miss Gill.

“I’m giving the next party a start,” ses Ginger.

The man in charge helped ’im out, and Miss Gill took ’is arm. She was very kind about it, and said that some of the bravest men couldn’t bear swinging. Ginger said he could bear it well enough, but he had eaten something at tea which disagreed with ’im.

They walked along quiet for a bit, and then Miss Gill sighed.

Ginger heard it and waited.

She sighed agin.

“Anything wrong?” he ses.

“No,” she ses, quick. “Nothing.”

Ginger waited till she had done it a third time.

“You’re unhappy,” he ses. “I can tell.”

“It’s only a little trouble,” she ses.

“Tell me,” ses Ginger.

“I couldn’t.”

“Why not?”

“It wouldn’t be right.”

Ginger stopped walking.

“Anything that troubles you concerns me,” he ses.

Miss Gill looked at ’im with tears in ’er eyes.

“You’re very good,” she ses. “Much too good.”

Ginger felt as if he had grown six inches. He led ’er to a quiet seat, and after saying she couldn’t tell ’im five or six times she told ’im. An aunt she lived with had trusted ’er to pay a bill of three pounds, and on the way she had lost the money. The bill had to be paid next morning, and her aunt was strict, and if she found out there was no knowing wot might happen.

“Is that all?” ses Ginger.

“All?” she ses. “Three pounds!”

“Three pounds ain’t much,” ses Ginger, though it was more than he had meant to spend in a week.

“It’s a fortune to me,” she ses. “I’ve tried everywhere.”

“Let me lend it to you,” ses Ginger.

Miss Gill drew back.

“Oh, no!”

“Why not?”

“I couldn’t take money from you.”

“I should be offended if you didn’t,” ses Ginger.

“It’s impossible.”

Ginger put ’is hand in his pocket and took out his purse. Miss Gill turned ’er head away.

“I can’t,” she ses.

“You must,” ses Ginger.

He counted three sovereigns into ’er hand, and she looked at ’em as if they was red-hot.

“I’ll pay you back,” she ses. “Every penny.”

“There’s no hurry,” ses Ginger.

“I don’t know how to thank you.”

Ginger looked up and down the path. There was nobody close except an old gentleman asleep behind a newspaper.

“You could if you tried,” he ses.

Miss Gill lowered ’er eyes.

“Could I?” she ses.

Ginger put his arm round ’er waist and kissed ’er.

The next moment his cap was in the dust and ’is left ear felt as if somebody had shut a door on it. Miss Gill stood up, trembling all over.

“How dare you!” she ses.

Ginger opened ’is mouth, but nothing came out.

“You wicked, deceitful man!” she ses. “I trusted you.”

“But—but—” ses Ginger.

“Keeper!” ses Miss Gill.

The old gentleman woke up behind ’is newspaper and called “Keeper!” too, without knowing why. Two other people joined in, and afore Ginger could explain, a man in uniform had ’im by the arm.

“He insulted me,” ses Miss Gill, bursting into tears.

“I didn’t,” ses Ginger. “I only—”

“Out you go,” ses the keeper.

Ginger went. He tried to walk dignified, but the keeper’s hand between ’is shoulders interfered with it. At the gate he looked back and saw Miss Gill dabbing ’er eyes with one hand and holding tight to the three pounds with the other.

He got home at ten o’clock. Sam and Peter was waiting up for ’im.

“Well?” ses Sam.

Ginger hung up ’is cap.

“Pleasant day?” ses Peter.

“Fair,” ses Ginger.

“How did you get on?” ses Sam.

“Same as anybody else,” ses Ginger.

“Did she flirt with you?” ses Peter.

Ginger turned round very fierce.

“Flirt? Miss Gill? Certainly not. She’s one of the most modest gals I’ve ever met.”

Peter stared at ’im.

“I thought you was going to take ’er away from Joe,” he ses.

“I’ve changed my mind,” ses Ginger. “She’s devoted to ’im.”

“Did she tell you so?” ses Sam.

“She didn’t need to,” ses Ginger.

Peter looked at ’is ear.

“You’ve got a mark there,” he ses.

“Mosquito,” ses Ginger.

“In London?” ses Peter.

“It must have escaped from the insect-house,” ses Ginger. “And if you two have finished asking silly questions, I’m going to bed.”

He went upstairs, and Peter watched ’im.

“There’s something wrong,” he ses.

Sam nodded.

“He’s lost ’is three pounds,” he ses.

“How d’you know?”

“He counted ’is money afore he went out,” ses Sam, “and he’s been feeling ’is empty pocket ever since he come in.”

Next day Peter tried to get the truth out of ’im, but Ginger wouldn’t say nothing except that Miss Gill was a credit to her sex. The more he praised ’er, the more suspicious Peter became.

“You made a mess of it,” he ses at last.

“I didn’t try,” ses Ginger.

“You did.”

“I didn’t.”

“Then you won’t mind me trying,” ses Peter.

Ginger looked at ’im.

“You?”

“Yes, me,” ses Peter. “I bet you a sovereign I take ’er out and she likes it.”

“You couldn’t get ’er to come,” ses Ginger.

“I bet I can.”

Ginger thought it over. He wanted to warn Peter, but he couldn’t do that without telling the truth, and the thought of Peter coming home with a red ear comforted ’im.

“Done,” he ses.

Peter arranged it through Joe, same as Ginger had done. He said he wanted Miss Gill’s advice about a birthday present for Sam’s sister, and Joe, who seemed anxious to help everybody, fixed it up for Saturday.

Peter chose the Crystal Palace. He wore ’is velvet-collared coat and carried a walking-stick which he had bought that morning. Ginger advised ’im not to swing it where there was elephants about, but Peter merely smiled.

Miss Gill met ’im looking prettier than ever. She was a little shy at first, but Peter told ’er that he wasn’t like Ginger.

“In wot way?” she ses.

“All ways,” ses Peter.

“He’s very kind,” she ses.

“Kind enough,” ses Peter. “But not clever.”

“He seems clever.”

“That’s because he talks fast,” ses Peter. “A clever man don’t ’ave to hurry.”

Miss Gill said she had never thought of that, and looked at Peter so admiring that he began to walk slower.

They went through the Palace and saw nearly everything. Peter explained the statues and pictures to ’er, making it up as he went along, and Miss Gill listened without smiling. At a model of an ancient temple he told ’er it had been discovered by Captain Cook in Egypt, and she said it was wonderful how much sailors knew.

At the rifle gallery Peter said shooting was ’is special gift. He fired six shots and missed the target five times. The sixth hit a little tin bird belonging to the next gallery, and the proprietor made ’im pay fourpence damages.

“The sights are wrong,” ses Peter.

“Of course,” ses Miss Gill.

He tried agin and knocked a clay pipe out of the attendant’s mouth. After that they went somewhere quieter.

At dinner Peter ordered more than he could eat and pressed delicacies on Miss Gill till she said she couldn’t swallow another mouthful. Then she ate two ices and a bag of chocolates while they listened to the band.

“You’ve made me very happy,” she ses.

Peter twirled ’is moustache.

“I generally do,” he ses.

“I mean,” she ses, “I was miserable when I came.”

“Miserable?” ses Peter.

“I oughtn’t to say anything.”

Peter put on a sympathetic look.

“You can trust me,” he ses. “I’m different from most men.”

“I know that,” she ses.

Peter moved closer.

“It’s only a little money trouble,” she ses. “But I’d rather not speak of it.”

Peter’s face changed for half a second, and then he smiled.

“How much?” he ses.

“Three pounds,” she ses, in a whisper.

“Three pounds?” ses Peter.

Miss Gill nodded, and a tear rolled down ’er cheek.

Peter stared at the band. He had heard something very like it afore, though Ginger had been careful not to tell ’im. He began to wonder whether Ginger had lent ’er three pounds too, and then he remembered the bet and the way Ginger would laugh if he came home without getting farther than this.

“I’ve got three pounds,” he ses.

Miss Gill shook ’er head.

“I couldn’t borrow from you.”

“Why not?”

“It might spoil our friendship.”

“Nothing could do that,” ses Peter.

“It wouldn’t be right.”

Peter took out three sovereigns. He held ’em for a moment, as though hoping one of ’em might turn out to be a button, and then placed ’em in ’er hand.

“There,” he ses.

Miss Gill looked at ’im with wet eyes.

“You’ve saved me,” she ses.

Peter looked round. There was a lot of people about, so he suggested a stroll outside. Miss Gill went with ’im, and presently they came to a quiet path with bushes on both sides.

“I don’t know how to thank you,” she ses.

Peter thought that sounded familiar too, though he couldn’t remember where he had heard it.

“There are ways,” he ses.

Miss Gill looked down.

Peter put his walking-stick under one arm, took ’er hand, and bent towards ’er.

He came home at eleven with no walking-stick and a scratch down one cheek. Ginger and Sam was playing cards.

“Well?” ses Ginger.

Peter took off ’is overcoat.

“Splendid,” he ses.

“Enjoy yourself?” ses Sam.

“Never had a better day,” ses Peter.

Ginger looked at the scratch.

“Mosquito?” he ses.

“No,” ses Peter. “Tiger.”

“At the Crystal Palace?”

“Model tiger,” ses Peter. “Very lifelike.”

“Did she flirt with you?” ses Ginger.

Peter laughed scornful.

“A lady like that?” he ses. “You ought to be ashamed.”

“Did you kiss ’er?” ses Ginger.

Peter’s face got red.

“A gentleman doesn’t talk about such things,” he ses.

“You didn’t,” ses Ginger.

Peter pulled a sovereign out of ’is pocket and tossed it on the table.

“There’s the bet,” he ses.

Ginger picked it up.

“So you failed,” he ses.

“I only said I’d take ’er out and she’d like it,” ses Peter. “She said she’d never been so happy.”

“That don’t mean nothing,” ses Ginger.

“It means more than anything she said to you,” ses Peter.

They began arguing, and in two minutes each was calling the other a liar. Sam separated ’em and asked Peter how much money he had left.

“That’s my business,” ses Peter.

“You lent ’er three pounds,” ses Ginger, sudden.

Peter stared.

“’Ow did you know?” he ses.

Ginger jumped up.

“She got three off you too?”

Peter looked at Ginger, and Ginger looked at Peter. Then they both looked away.

“She had a little difficulty,” ses Peter.

“Lost some money?” ses Ginger.

“Yes.”

“Belonging to an aunt?”

Peter nodded.

“Bill due next morning?” ses Ginger.

Peter nodded agin.

There was a long silence.

“Did she slap you?” ses Ginger.

Peter drew himself up.

“Certainly not,” he ses.

Ginger waited.

“Well—not exactly,” ses Peter. “She caught me with ’er hand accidental.”

“Three times?” ses Ginger.

“Twice,” ses Peter. “The third was with my own walking-stick.”

Sam dropped into a chair and laughed till the tears ran down ’is face. Ginger told ’im to shut up, and Peter said he’d knock ’is head off if he didn’t. Sam tried to stop, but every time he looked at their faces he started agin.

“You pair of experienced men,” he ses. “You judges of women!”

“She’s a swindler,” ses Ginger.

“A dangerous criminal,” ses Peter. “We ought to tell Joe.”

“And tell ’im wot?” ses Sam. “That each of you tried to take ’is gal away, lent ’er three pounds, and got slapped for your trouble?”

“It was for ’is good,” ses Ginger.

“Course,” ses Sam. “And the kissing?”

“That was evidence,” ses Peter.

They was still discussing it next evening when Joe came in. He looked happier than ever, and he had a small parcel under ’is arm.

“I’ve come to show you something,” he ses.

Ginger and Peter stopped talking.

“Miss Gill bought me a present,” ses Joe.

He opened the parcel and took out a silver watch with a handsome chain. Then he held up ’is other hand, and there was a gold ring on ’is little finger.

“She gave me the ring too,” he ses. “Ain’t it a beauty?”

Sam took the watch and examined it.

“Must have cost a bit,” he ses.

“Six pounds the lot,” ses Joe, proud-like. “Three for the watch and chain, and three for the ring. She’s been saving up for months. That’s wot I call affection.”

Nobody spoke.

Joe looked at Ginger.

“She says she enjoyed the Zoological Gardens,” he ses. “She told me you was very generous.”

Ginger made a noise in ’is throat.

“And she liked the Crystal Palace too,” Joe went on. “She says Peter is a real gentleman.”

Peter buttoned his coat up to the chin.

“She’s a wonderful gal,” ses Joe. “She never spends money on herself. You don’t meet many like ’er.”

“No,” ses Sam. “You don’t.”

Joe held out the watch.

“Listen to it,” he ses. “Goes beautiful.”

They listened. It ticked away cheerful as anything.

“Six pounds,” ses Ginger, very slow.

“Six pounds,” ses Joe. “And she made me promise never to ask where she got it.”

Ginger turned and looked at Peter.

Peter looked at Ginger.

Then Ginger ses, “She slapped me.”

Peter rubbed the scratch on ’is cheek.

“She slapped me too,” he ses.

And Joe, thinking they was talking about somebody else, held the watch to ’is ear and said it was a funny thing how unlucky some men was with women.

The Clockmaker of Bellweather

Every clock in Bellweather stopped at 3:17 on the morning the sea disappeared.

Pendulums froze mid-swing. Pocket watches fell silent in waistcoats hung over chairs. The great brass clock in the railway station held its minute hand above the third notch, though the last train had passed through the town nearly twenty years before. Even the kitchen clock in Mara Venn’s house, which had always run seven minutes fast, stopped at precisely the same moment as all the others.

Mara did not notice until dawn.

She woke to silence. Not ordinary silence, with gulls crying over the roofs and waves striking the seawall below the cliffs, but a deep, padded stillness. It seemed to press against the windows.

She left her narrow bed, pulled on her boots, and went downstairs to the workshop.

Her grandfather was already there.

Orin Venn sat at his workbench, surrounded by open clocks. Springs and gears lay in careful rows beneath the yellow lamplight. His silver hair was untidy, and he wore a magnifying lens over one eye.

“Grandfather,” Mara said, “the clocks have stopped.”

“I know.”

“All of them?”

“All of them.”

He did not look surprised. That frightened her more than the silence.

Mara crossed the workshop and opened the front door.

Bellweather stood on a cliff above the Northern Sea. For as long as anyone remembered, the sea had been visible at the end of every street: a dark, restless line beneath the sky. Fishermen measured their lives by its tides. Children learned to swim before they learned to read. Salt whitened the houses, corroded hinges, and settled into bread.

But that morning, beyond the seawall, there was no water.

The sea had withdrawn past the horizon.

Where it had been lay a plain of wet sand, black stone, and silver pools stretching beneath a colorless sky. Stranded boats leaned on their sides. Fish twisted weakly in the mud. Far in the distance, things that had been hidden for centuries glimmered in the gray light: towers, roads, and the broken roofs of a drowned city.

The townspeople gathered along the seawall.

Some prayed. Some shouted. A group of fishermen climbed down the cliff path with buckets, already arguing about who owned the exposed seabed. Mayor Holt rang the town bell until its rope broke, though no sound came from the bronze mouth.

Mara turned to her grandfather.

“What happened?”

Orin removed the lens from his eye.

“Something has taken the tide,” he said.

“That isn’t possible.”

“Neither is a town full of stopped clocks.”

He reached beneath his workbench and brought out a wooden box. Mara had seen it before but had never known what it contained. It was made of dark wood, bound with green copper, and marked with the image of a heron holding a key in its beak.

Orin opened it.

Inside lay a watch.

It was larger than an ordinary pocket watch and black as coal. Its face had no numbers. Instead, twelve tiny symbols circled a single silver hand: a shell, a flame, a closed eye, a crown, a door, and others Mara did not recognize. The hand pointed to the symbol of an empty cup.

Unlike every other clock in Bellweather, the watch was ticking.

Mara leaned closer.

“What is it?”

“The Tidekeeper.”

“Who made it?”

“I did,” Orin said. “A very long time ago.”

Mara stared at him. Her grandfather had been old all her life, but not impossibly old. The watch looked ancient. Its case was worn smooth, and fine grains of sand clung beneath its glass.

Orin closed the box.

“There is a place beneath the sea called Lyr,” he said. “Before Bellweather was built, Lyr stood on this coast. Its people learned to bind time into machines. Not merely hours and minutes, but seasons, memories, even promises. They believed anything could be preserved if given a mechanism strong enough.”

“And you lived there?”

“Yes.”

Mara wanted to laugh. Instead, she looked through the open door at the drowned towers rising from the exposed seabed.

“What happened to it?”

“We tried to preserve too much.”

Orin’s voice softened.

“At the center of Lyr was a machine called the Heart Clock. It governed the tides. We built it because storms had taken too many ships and too many children. At first, it worked. We could slow the sea, calm it, command it to retreat. Then the king ordered us to stop time around the city so Lyr would never decay.”

He paused.

“Time does not enjoy being commanded. The Heart Clock failed. The sea rose. Lyr sank. Only a few escaped.”

“And now the sea is gone because the machine has started again?”

“Not started,” Orin said. “It has been winding itself for three hundred years. Last night, it reached the end.”

“What happens next?”

“At sunset, the Heart Clock will release everything it has held back.”

Mara looked again at the endless plain.

“The sea will return.”

“All at once.”

Bellweather would vanish beneath it.

Orin stood, but his hands trembled against the bench. Only then did Mara see how pale he was.

“You must go to Lyr,” he said.

“Me?”

“The Heart Clock can be stopped with the Tidekeeper. But the road is long, and my heart is no longer suited to hurrying.”

“Then I’ll help you.”

“You cannot help an old man move faster than his bones.”

“And you cannot expect me to find a machine in a drowned city I’ve never seen.”

Orin pushed the wooden box into her hands.

“The watch will guide you. Follow the silver hand. When you reach the Heart Clock, place the Tidekeeper into its center. Then turn the crown backward until the mechanism stops.”

“That sounds too simple.”

“It is simple,” he said. “Simple things are not always easy.”

Outside, the town erupted in cheers. The fishermen had discovered chests scattered among the wrecks below the cliff. Men and women rushed down with carts, shovels, ropes, and sacks. Even Mayor Holt joined them, his coat flapping behind him.

“Shouldn’t we warn them?” Mara asked.

“I have tried.”

Orin nodded toward the street.

On the wall beside the shop door hung a notice written in his precise hand:

THE SEA WILL RETURN AT SUNSET. LEAVE BELLWEATHER. SEEK HIGH GROUND.

Someone had drawn a smiling fish beneath it.

“People believe warnings only when danger has already arrived,” Orin said.

Mara put the box into her satchel. She took a coil of rope, a hammer, two bottles of water, and the loaf of bread left from supper. At the door, she turned.

“What if I fail?”

Her grandfather lowered himself into his chair.

“Then try to be somewhere beautiful when the sea returns.”

The journey across the seabed began easily.

Mara followed the old harbor road, passing stranded fishing boats and townspeople gathering coins from the mud. Children chased crabs through shallow pools. Merchants inspected barnacled statues and spoke excitedly of museums and collectors.

As Mara walked farther, the voices faded.

The seabed was not flat. Deep channels cut through it, and hills of black rock rose like the backs of buried animals. Thick weeds clung to her boots. The air smelled of salt, rot, and storms.

The Tidekeeper’s silver hand moved whenever she changed direction. It led her east, toward the drowned city.

By midmorning, she reached the first ruins.

A stone arch stood alone in the mud. Beyond it stretched a road paved with white shells. Houses leaned against one another, their windows crowded with anemones. Water dripped from balconies carved in the shapes of wings.

Mara imagined people walking there beneath banners, carrying baskets, calling to friends. She imagined Orin as a young man hurrying through those streets with tools in his pockets.

She had gone only a few steps beneath the arch when a voice called, “Wait!”

A boy scrambled over a mound of coral behind her.

He was perhaps fourteen, two years younger than Mara, with a red scarf around his neck and a canvas sack on his back. Mara recognized him as Tovan Reed, the son of a fisherman. He had a reputation for stealing apples, sleeping through sermons, and once setting fire to the mayor’s privy.

“You shouldn’t be here,” Mara said.

“Neither should you.”

“I have work to do.”

“So do I.”

He opened his sack. It contained six tarnished goblets, a silver plate, and the jeweled hilt of a sword.

“You’re robbing the dead.”

“They aren’t using any of it.”

“The sea will return at sunset.”

“I heard your grandfather’s warning.”

“And?”

Tovan shrugged.

“My father says Orin Venn has breathed clock oil for so long that his thoughts have turned into gears.”

“Then go back.”

“I would, but I saw you heading here with no treasure sack and a very serious face. That usually means something interesting is happening.”

“It means something dangerous is happening.”

“Even better.”

Mara walked on. Tovan followed.

She tried ignoring him, then insulting him, then threatening to strike him with the hammer. None worked.

“You’ll get lost without me,” he said. “I know how to read the old fishermen’s maps.”

“This city isn’t on any fishermen’s map.”

“Then you’ll get lost with me, which is friendlier.”

The Tidekeeper led them toward the center of Lyr.

The deeper they went, the taller the ruins became. They crossed gardens filled with glass trees and passed a temple whose stone doors opened and closed with the wind. In a public square, hundreds of statues stood facing a dry fountain. Each statue had the same expression: eyes raised, mouth open, as if watching a great wave descend.

At noon, the ground trembled.

A low roar rolled across the seabed.

Mara climbed a fallen column and looked back toward Bellweather. Along the horizon, a thin blue line had appeared.

The sea was returning.

Not quickly yet, but it was returning.

“We should go back,” Tovan said.

“You should.”

“You keep saying that as if I’m going to listen.”

They ate bread while walking. The watch guided them through a market and down a staircase into darkness.

Mara lit the small oil lamp in her satchel.

They entered a tunnel lined with metal pipes. Some were no wider than her finger; others were large enough to crawl through. Within them came a faint whispering.

Tovan put his ear against one.

“Voices,” he said.

Mara listened.

At first, she heard only the hiss of trapped air. Then words emerged.

Come home before dark.

Don’t forget the blue ribbon.

I forgive you.

A woman’s laughter followed, bright and distant.

Mara stepped back.

“What is this place?”

“The people of Lyr stored memories in machines,” she said, recalling Orin’s explanation. “Perhaps these are some of them.”

Tovan moved to another pipe.

His face changed.

“What do you hear?” Mara asked.

“Nothing.”

But he continued listening until she pulled him away.

They went deeper. The whispers followed them, mixing into a soft chorus. Some spoke with love, others with anger. A mother sang to a child. A dying man asked someone to open a window. A girl promised to wait on a bridge.

The tunnel ended at a circular door.

Its center held a hollow the size of the Tidekeeper.

Mara placed the watch inside.

The door opened with a sigh.

Beyond it lay a chamber filled with clocks.

Thousands covered the walls, floor, and ceiling. Some were made of gold, others of bone, crystal, or dark wood. There were clocks with thirteen hands, clocks whose faces showed changing landscapes, and tiny clocks beating like insect wings.

All were stopped.

As Mara and Tovan crossed the chamber, the Tidekeeper began ticking faster.

At the far end stood three doors.

The first was painted with a shell, the second with a crown, and the third with an open eye.

The silver hand pointed to the crown.

Mara reached for the handle.

“Wait,” Tovan said. “The watch told us where to go before. But this place was built by people who trapped promises in pipes. Maybe following directions blindly is unwise.”

“Do you have a better idea?”

He examined the doors.

Above them, nearly hidden beneath barnacles, were carved words. Mara wiped them clean.

WHAT THE SEA GIVES, THE CROWN TAKES.

WHAT THE CROWN HIDES, THE EYE REVEALS.

WHAT THE EYE FEARS, THE SEA KEEPS.

“The watch points to the crown,” Mara said.

“Yes, but what does the crown take?”

“Whatever the sea gives.”

“And what has the sea given us?”

Mara thought of fish, salt, storms, and the city itself. Then she understood.

“Time.”

She looked down at the Tidekeeper. Its hand did not point toward safety. It pointed toward what the Heart Clock was doing.

The crown door would take their remaining time.

She chose the door painted with the open eye.

Behind it was a bridge.

It stretched across a vast underground chasm. Far below, gears larger than houses turned slowly in darkness. There was no railing. The bridge’s stones were slick with seawater.

Halfway across, Tovan stopped.

“Mara.”

A wall of water had entered the clock chamber behind them. It crashed through the three doors, pouring into the chasm.

The sea had reached Lyr.

“Run!” Mara shouted.

They ran.

Water swept around their ankles, then their knees. The bridge shook as ancient machinery awakened below. One of the enormous gears turned with a deafening groan.

Tovan slipped.

Mara caught his wrist, but his canvas sack dragged him toward the edge. Goblets and coins spilled into the darkness.

“Let go of the sack!” she yelled.

“It’s caught!”

She pulled the hammer from her belt and cut through the strap with its claw. The treasure vanished into the gears. Freed from its weight, Tovan climbed back onto the bridge.

They reached the other side as the bridge collapsed.

The Tidekeeper now pointed straight ahead.

They climbed a spiral staircase while water thundered below. At the top, they emerged into the highest tower in Lyr.

The Heart Clock filled it.

It was larger than Orin’s entire shop. Rings of brass rotated around a sphere of blue glass. Water moved inside the sphere, though there were no pipes connected to it. Lightning flashed in its depths.

Twelve iron figures stood around the machine, each holding a chain. Kings, queens, priests, and clockmakers—all bowed beneath the strain.

One figure had Orin’s face.

Mara approached it.

He was carved as a young man, but there was no mistaking his sharp nose and deep-set eyes. The iron Orin held a key in one hand and a broken crown in the other.

“He helped build this,” she whispered.

The tower shook.

Through the windows, Mara saw water flooding the streets. It rose over houses and temples, turning roads into rivers. The distant cliffs of Bellweather were no longer visible.

“Where does the watch go?” Tovan asked.

They searched the Heart Clock. At last Mara found a round opening beneath the glass sphere.

She inserted the Tidekeeper.

The machine stopped.

For one breath, everything was silent.

Then a voice spoke.

“Mara Venn.”

It came from the blue sphere.

A shape appeared inside: a woman with long dark hair floating around her face. Her eyes were the same gray as Mara’s.

“Who are you?” Mara asked.

“The last keeper of Lyr.”

The woman placed her hand against the inside of the glass.

“And the first daughter of Orin Venn.”

Mara could not speak.

“My mother?” she managed.

“Your mother’s mother, many times removed. Blood is a road, Mara. Long, but unbroken.”

The silver crown of the Tidekeeper rose from its case.

“Turn it backward,” Tovan said.

But the woman in the sphere smiled sadly.

“If you do, the Heart Clock will release its hold. The sea will return to its natural course.”

“That’s what we want.”

“Bellweather was built where the sea once stood. In its natural course, the water will cover the town.”

Mara looked through the window. The waves were already racing toward the cliffs.

“Can the town be saved?”

“Yes. Turn the crown forward. The sea will retreat again, and Bellweather will remain. But the Heart Clock must be tended by a living keeper.”

“For how long?”

“Until time ends.”

Tovan stepped beside her.

“No.”

The woman ignored him.

“You are of Orin’s blood. The machine will accept you. You will not age. You will not hunger. You will keep the sea beneath your hand, and everyone in Bellweather will live.”

Mara imagined the workshop at dusk, lamplight warming the windows. She imagined Orin waiting beside the silent clocks. She imagined fishermen, children, and the foolish mayor. All could be saved.

She placed her fingers on the crown.

“What happened to the other keepers?” she asked.

The woman’s face drifted closer.

“They remained.”

“Inside the clock?”

“They became part of its memory.”

Mara understood then. The woman was not alive. She was an echo, like the voices in the pipes. A promise preserved so perfectly that it did not know it had been broken.

“How many people did Lyr sacrifice to keep itself safe?” Mara asked.

The woman’s expression did not change.

“As many as necessary.”

“And was it ever enough?”

Outside, a tower disappeared beneath the waves.

Mara thought of her grandfather, who had escaped the city but carried its guilt for three hundred years. He had not sent her to preserve his work. He had sent her to end it.

“Backward,” she said.

She turned the crown.

The Heart Clock screamed.

Every clock in the tower began striking at once. The iron figures shattered. The brass rings spun faster, shedding sparks. Cracks spread across the blue sphere.

The woman inside pressed both hands against the glass.

“You will destroy Bellweather!”

“No,” Mara said. “I’m giving it back its future.”

The sphere broke.

Water exploded through the chamber.

Tovan seized Mara’s arm as the floor tilted beneath them. They were swept through a window and into the rising sea.

The world became cold and green.

Mara lost the Tidekeeper. She saw it sinking below her, its silver hand spinning freely. Then Tovan pulled her upward.

They broke the surface among rooftops.

The tower of the Heart Clock collapsed behind them, sending a wave through the city. Mara grabbed a floating wooden door. She and Tovan clung to it as the current carried them over Lyr.

For a long time, there was only water.

Then they saw boats.

The fishermen of Bellweather had finally understood Orin’s warning. They had abandoned their treasure and launched every vessel they could. Small boats crowded the sea, filled with townspeople. Some had escaped to the hills above the cliffs; others had been caught by the flood and pulled from rooftops.

A fishing boat hauled Mara and Tovan aboard.

“Bellweather?” Mara asked.

The fisherman looked away.

The town was gone.

Only the church steeple and the upper floor of the railway station remained above water. Mara’s home, the workshop, the seawall, and every salt-whitened street had disappeared.

“Orin?” she whispered.

No one answered.

At sunset, the clocks began again.

Across the boats, watches ticked in wet pockets. The railway clock, standing above the waves, moved from 3:17 to 3:18.

The sea settled into a gentle tide.

Years later, people built a new Bellweather farther inland.

They used stone recovered from the old town and timber brought down from the northern forests. The fishermen made a new harbor. The mayor, humbled and permanently unpopular, ordered warning bells placed on every hill.

Mara opened a clock shop in the new town.

Above its door hung a wooden sign carved with a heron holding a key in its beak. Tovan worked across the street as a mapmaker, though his maps often included sea monsters in places where no sea monsters had been reported.

On quiet mornings, Mara repaired watches at the same workbench her grandfather had used. It had washed ashore after the flood, scarred but intact. In its smallest drawer, she found a note written in Orin’s hand.

There are things we preserve from love and things we preserve from fear. Learn the difference.

Mara kept the note beneath her tools.

Sometimes divers came to her with objects recovered from the drowned ruins: crystal gears, rusted keys, scraps of metal that whispered when held to the ear. She locked such things in iron boxes and refused to repair them.

Once, many years after the flood, a child brought her a black watch found on the beach.

Its face had no numbers. Twelve symbols circled a single silver hand.

The Tidekeeper was silent.

“Can you make it work?” the child asked.

Mara held the watch to her ear.

Deep inside, something shifted.

For an instant she heard waves, bells, and a woman’s voice calling her name from the other side of time.

Then all was still.

“Yes,” Mara said, closing the case. “I think I could.”

The child smiled.

Mara walked to the cliff and threw the watch into the sea.

It flashed once beneath the sunlight before the water took it.

Behind her, the clocks of Bellweather struck noon—not perfectly together, but near enough. Their bells overlapped in a bright confusion of sound.

Mara listened until the final note faded.

Then she returned to her shop, where a dozen broken clocks waited to be given not more time, but the right amount.
